title: "From Activities to Impact: Why Managing for Results Is No Longer Optional in Public Sector Governance"

### **Responding to citizens’ and stakeholders’ demands for evidence, accountability, and measurable development outcomes**

**Haven Wesseh Yarl, October 21, 2026**

On December 30, 2025, a former Liberian Minister of Finance and Development Planning appeared on a local radio and live TV talk show (Spoon Talk) to discuss the previous administration’s performance. As former head of the Economic Management Team and coordinator of the country’s national development plan, he was asked about its achievements, lessons learned, and contributions to growth, poverty reduction, and economic stability, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.

I listened closely, both as a citizen and as someone who once worked at the Ministry, where I helped coordinate and track two (2) post-war national development plans and an economic recovery plan following the Ebola outbreak. Like many listeners and viewers, I expected a detailed, persuasive account of results. The conversation was engaging and insightful, but one moment stood out. When asked how government programs had changed people’s lives and how many had escaped poverty during his six (6) years in office, the former official could not provide solid, verifiable evidence. The issue wasn't a lack of effort or results, but the absence of clear data showing what had been achieved.

The debate carried on in local talk shows over the next few days. To me, this showed that public expectations of government action are changing rapidly. People now want more than just reports or explanations of what the government spent, built, or started. They want to know what really changed, and who benefited.

This challenge is not unique to Liberia. Governments, especially in developing countries, often report budget figures, the number of schools built, clinics opened, and roads paved. But the bigger questions remain: Did children learn more? Did patients get healthier? Did farmers reach new markets? Did household incomes increase? How many people were lifted out of poverty, and can we clearly link those changes to specific policies or programs?

Political speeches or a few success stories about deliverables are not enough to answer these questions. We need solid data, careful analysis, and open reporting. Public governance should move beyond counting activities and focus on real results, learning from what works, and using evidence to make decisions. This is what Managing for Results (MfR) is all about.

This does not mean that building infrastructure or providing services is unimportant. Building a school is valuable, but it matters even more if students attend, stay enrolled, and learn. Expanding health centers is needed, but the real test is whether fewer people die from preventable causes. Roads and electricity are essential, but the key question is whether they help people access opportunities, become more productive, and improve their lives. MfR links resources and activities to results and long-term impacts, so governments can show not just what they did, but what difference it made.

Making MfR part of how things work takes more than just gathering statistics. It means linking national goals to sector results and program outputs, setting clear starting points and targets, regularly checking progress, and figuring out what works, for whom, and under what conditions. Evidence should guide changes: keep what works, fix what doesn’t, and move resources when results are lacking.

A working MfR system also makes public officials more accountable. It helps them answer the public’s questions with real evidence, supports lawmakers in checking budgets, and makes it easier to track progress toward national goals and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Just as important, it allows space to admit mistakes, learn openly, and make changes before more resources and chances are wasted.

The need for this change is clearer than ever. War in Europe and conflict in the Middle East are disrupting lives, trade, and government budgets. Threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are driving up energy, transport, and food costs, affecting families far from the conflict. At the same time, donor countries are shifting spending priorities, development aid is under pressure, and funding cuts are making it harder for parts of the United Nations and the wider humanitarian system to do their work. For countries already facing poverty, debt, climate shocks, and weak services, these challenges mean that needs are growing while resources are becoming less reliable.

In this environment, every public dollar and every bit of international aid matters more. Governments and their partners must distinguish what is truly urgent from what merely looks busy; what changes lives from what only creates activity; and what should continue from what needs to change. Managing for Results cannot stop wars, replace lost funding, or fix every big problem. But it can help protect key services, focus limited resources on real needs, reveal gaps, and build the trust needed to make tough decisions.

In the end, the real question is not whether governments can afford to manage for results, but whether people can afford governments that do not. Every budget line represents a family waiting for medicine, a young person looking for a chance, or a child whose future depends on a working school. In these times of conflict, uncertainty, and tighter budgets, governments should measure development outcomes by changes in lives, not just activity counts. Results are not just numbers in a report. They show the real impact of public decisions and actions on people’s lives.
